title: Young Indian Wrestlers Denied US Visas Ahead of U23 World Championships in Las Vegas
excerpt: Nine of 16 Indian wrestlers who appeared for visa interviews at the US Embassy in New Delhi were refused on Wednesday — told they were below 20 and unemployed; the WFI has asked the embassy to reconsider ahead of Thursday’s appointments.
body:
• Nine Indian wrestlers were refused US visas on Wednesday at the US Embassy in New Delhi, putting India's participation in the U23 World Wrestling Championships in Las Vegas (October 12–18) in doubt. Of 24 squad participants who appeared for appointments, 16 were wrestlers — and 9 of them were turned down.
  • The wrestlers — including 2024 U17 world champion Neha Sangwan — were verbally told their applications were refused because they were below 20 years of age and unemployed. Their passports were returned at the interviews.
  • The Wrestling Federation of India has urged the embassy to reconsider, arguing the U23 championship is for athletes aged 18–23 who are pursuing sporting careers rather than formal employment — and warning that most wrestlers with Thursday appointments face the same profile.
  • This is not the first time visa trouble has hit an Indian wrestling squad: in 2022, Spain denied visas to 21 Indian wrestlers for the U23 Worlds in Pontevedra on similar overstay suspicions.

Indian wrestling's next generation has run into a wall before even reaching the mat. Nine Indian wrestlers were refused US visas on Wednesday at the US Embassy in New Delhi, just days before the U23 World Wrestling Championships open in Las Vegas — prompting the Wrestling Federation of India to seek an urgent review.

According to the WFI's letter to the embassy, quoted by PTI: "Today, 24 participants appeared at the Embassy for their visa appointments, out of which 16 were wrestlers. Unfortunately, 09 wrestlers were refused visas, reportedly due to their employment status and are below 20 years of age."

Who was turned down — and why

The nine wrestlers named in the WFI's communication are Samarth Gajanan Mhakave, Dheeraj Kumar Malik, Sachin Kumar, Nikhil, Hardeep, Parveen, Ahilya Shatrughn Shinde, Neha Sharma, and Neha Sangwan — the last a 2024 U17 world champion. The Times of India reported the story on October 7, 2026.

The wrestlers were verbally told their applications were refused because they were below 20 years of age and unemployed, and their passports were returned when they appeared for the interviews on Wednesday. That combination is the classic trigger for refusals under US immigration law's immigrant-intent presumption, which requires every visa applicant to convince the consular officer they will return home after their visit. For teenage athletes with no job, property or travel history to point to, clearing that bar can be difficult — even when they carry government clearances and an invitation from the sport's world governing body.

The WFI pushed back on the logic: the championship is for the under-23 age group, with participants aged 18–23, so most of these young athletes are still pursuing their sporting careers and are not formally employed. The federation also expressed deep concern about the wrestlers scheduled for appointments on Thursday, noting most of them are also currently unemployed and below 20 — raising the prospect of further refusals.

The stakes and the timing

The 2026 U23 World Championships run October 12–18 at the Thomas & Mack Center in Las Vegas — the first time the United States has hosted the U23 Worlds, and the first World Championships of any age group on American soil since 2015. More than 600 wrestlers are expected, and United World Wrestling's entry lists already include Indian competitors across the men's freestyle weight classes.

A familiar nightmare for Indian wrestling

Indian wrestling has lived through this exact scenario before. In October 2022, the Spanish Embassy denied visas to 21 members of India's 30-strong squad for the U23 World Championships in Pontevedra, on suspicion the wrestlers might overstay — despite the WFI presenting government clearance and an invitation from United World Wrestling. Only nine wrestlers made that trip, and it was the first time in the competition's history that India failed to field a full team.

Then, as now, the federation called the decision bizarre and high-handed, and took the matter to the world body. The recurrence four years later — this time at a tournament the United States itself is hosting — underscores how little protection sporting credentials offer against consular discretion.

Diaspora angle

For the Indian diaspora in the US, which turns out in force for wrestling events, the irony is sharp: a home-soil world championship that Indian fans in Las Vegas may watch without India's full squad. More broadly, the episode lands in a year when US visa scrutiny has tightened across categories — from student programs to work authorizations — and young Indians are feeling it first.

What's next

Everything now hinges on the embassy's response to the WFI's plea — and on Thursday's appointments for the wrestlers still in the queue. If reconsideration fails, India could head to Las Vegas shorthanded for the second U23 Worlds in a row, and the federation will again be left asking the world body why host nations keep shutting its athletes out.
